prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on a simple and beautiful idea: at the magic wavelength the light shifts of the two clock levels cancel, so thousands of atoms can be held in a lattice, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and interrogated at the same time. Katori proposed this and demonstrated it, and Ye's group carried it to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and used it to see gravitational redshift across millimetres. That is a genuinely new regime of measurement, and it lets us ask quantitative questions about the constancy of constants, about time dilation inside a single sample, and about new physics. The result has been reproduced and compared between independent laboratories at the 1e-18 level, which is exactly the kind of robustness I look for. Four members ranked it in their top three and six of eight ranked it at all, a broader base than any other shortlisted entry. The two-name attribution is clean.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is an advance in measurement precision rather than the discovery of a new phenomenon, and the prize lineage is crowded: Hall and Hansch (2005, the comb) and Wineland and Haroche (2012, single quantum systems and ion clocks) already cover adjacent ground. A sceptical colleague could say that going from 1e-15 to 1e-18 is an increment. Further, the formal redefinition of the second has not happened, and groups at NIST, PTB, Paris and elsewhere also contributed decisively to making lattice clocks work, so two names cannot capture the whole field.

responses.point: Stefan ranks B015 first because it improves the best instrument for time by two orders of magnitude over caesium and opens new ways of observing nature, with several independent laboratories confirming 1e-18 performance.
responses.response: I agree with the measurement criterion and with the evidence of independent confirmation, and as an atomic theorist I can add that the physics behind the 1e-18 level is not a small refinement: the magic-wavelength condition, the control of blackbody and lattice light shifts, and the many-body interactions in a degenerate Fermi gas all had to be understood. I would qualify one point. The ion-clock lineage you mention is the real difficulty, not a footnote, because the 2012 citation was about measuring and manipulating single quantum systems. So the citation must stress the lattice concept and the large number of atoms, which is what Katori and Ye did and Wineland did not.

responses.point: Olle ranks B015 only seventh, saying that the case rests on a new level of precision rather than a new principle, and that the Hall-Hansch and Wineland prizes are adjacent.
responses.response: I take this seriously and it is my main reservation as well, but I disagree that no new principle is involved. Trapping neutral atoms in a lattice at the magic wavelength removes the old trade-off between the number of atoms and the freedom from motional shifts, and that is a conceptual step, not only better engineering. The clocks have also already been used as scientific instruments, for gravitational redshift at millimetre scale and for constraints on drifts of constants. I accept that your own preference, topological insulators, is a discovery of a new state of matter, which is a different kind of merit, and I would not argue that precision measurement outranks it automatically.

responses.point: Goran ranks circuit QED first as an elegant light-matter coupling on a chip and the architecture behind superconducting processors, while noting the overlap with the 2025 prize and that Blais's exclusion is a real credit problem.
responses.response: I share your admiration for strong coupling of an artificial atom to a single photon, and I ranked it, but only seventh. My concern is the timing: the 2025 prize went to superconducting circuits only a year ago, and I would not want a second recognition for the same community before the committee has argued that circuit QED is a distinct discovery rather than a technology. Your own remark that the three-person trio leaves out Blais, the lead theory author, makes the attribution less clean than for B015. If the committee does wish to reward cavity-type physics in circuits, I would want that argument made explicitly rather than assumed.

responses.point: Mark puts IceCube first as a new observational window, and also ranks B015 third as a measurement technique opening a new regime with carefully controlled systematics.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of lattice clocks and I appreciate that you value controlled systematics. On IceCube, I defer to you and Ulf on astroparticle physics, but my worry is the same as the one you raise: crediting Halzen alone for a collaboration of that size, with the AMANDA lineage behind it, makes the attribution much harder than for two named clock builders. I would also ask whether the source identification is firm enough to speak of astronomy. If the committee finds a solid answer to the solo-credit problem I would listen, but today I do not think it beats a clock prize with a clean pair of laureates.

uncertainties: How the committee weighs a precision-metrology achievement against a discovery of a new phenomenon, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes in adjacent areas.
Whether the SI redefinition of the second, still pending, should be awaited or whether the demonstrated 1e-18 performance is sufficient on its own.
Whether a clean two-name credit adequately reflects the contributions of other clock groups, for example at NIST, PTB and Paris.
If the committee wants a second part, I am unsure which pairing is both distinct and balanced, since Zoller and Cirac recur in B011 and B016 and would constrain the choice.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the shortlisted candidates is apparent from my profile. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate, and I have co-authored with Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of the shortlisted candidates concerns attosecond physics, and I have no stated link to Katori, Ye or the other credited names. I flag that my research field is atomic many-body theory, adjacent to the clock and cold-atom entries, which should be understood as expertise and not as a conflict.
